title: Idioms, Phrases, Proverbs, Similes & Phrasal Verbs
why: The 2022 IPO paper spent 12 of its 50 English questions on fixed expressions: 5 "complete the phrase" items, 5 "meaning of the idiom" items and 2 similes ("as ___ as a peacock"). These are pure recall questions, so each idiom you learn is a potential 2 marks in under 10 seconds. The same list also helps in sentence completion and comprehension.

lessons.title: How idiom questions are asked
lessons.body:
An **idiom** is a fixed group of words whose meaning is not the sum of its words: *to kick the bucket* = to die. A **proverb** is a complete traditional saying: *Too many cooks spoil the broth*. A **simile** compares with "as … as" or "like": *as busy as a bee*. A **phrasal verb** is verb + particle with a new meaning: *put off* = postpone.

### The four IPO formats
1. **Meaning of the idiom**: "Choose the option which best expresses the meaning of: *At sixes and sevens*."
2. **Complete the phrase/proverb**: "A bird in the hand is worth two in the ___."
3. **Simile fill-in**: "He was as ___ as a mule."
4. **Idiom/phrasal verb in a sentence**: "The match was *called off*." What does the underlined part mean?

### Strategy
- **Reject the literal option first.** Examiners always put one option that takes the words literally ("To tie a packet securely" for *tie the knot*). Idioms are almost never literal.
- **Use the tone.** Is the idiom positive or negative? *Crocodile tears* is clearly negative (fake), so a positive option is out.
- **For completions, the word is fixed by tradition.** It is "a stitch in time saves **nine**", never "ten". Do not pick a "logical" synonym.
- **Idioms change tense and pronoun, never nouns.** *He buried the hatchet*, *she has burnt her boats*. But never "bury the axe".

*Let sleeping dogs lie* and *Once bitten, twice shy* are in the proverbs table in the next lesson.

> **Classical idioms** carry their stories: **Achilles' heel** (weak point; Achilles could be wounded only in his heel), **Herculean task** (Hercules' twelve labours), **Midas touch** (King Midas turned everything to gold), **Pandora's box** (opening it released all evils), **Sword of Damocles** (a sword hung by a single hair over Damocles' head), **Trojan horse** (Greek soldiers hid inside a wooden horse), **Between Scylla and Charybdis** (two sea monsters, so two equal dangers).

lessons.title: Proverbs: complete the saying
lessons.body:
The blank is usually the **last word**. Learn the exact wording.

| Birds of a feather flock **together** | similar people keep company |
| We'll cross that **bridge** when we come to it | deal with a problem only when it arises |
| A bird in the hand is worth two in the **bush** | a sure thing beats a possible one |
| Too many cooks spoil the **broth** | too many people in charge ruin work |
| All that glitters is not **gold** | appearances deceive |
| Actions speak louder than **words** | deeds matter more than promises |
| Make hay while the **sun** shines | use an opportunity while it lasts |
| Don't count your chickens before they **hatch** | don't rely on something before it happens |
| Don't put all your eggs in one **basket** | don't risk everything on one venture |
| Strike while the iron is **hot** | act at the right moment |
| Rome was not built in a **day** | great work takes time |
| Where there's a will, there's a **way** | determination finds a method |

lessons.title: Similes: as ___ as a ___
lessons.body:
The pairings are fixed by convention. The quality usually matches a well-known feature of the thing (bees are busy, owls look wise, mules are stubborn).

| Simile | Simile | Simile |
|---|---|---|
| as proud as a peacock | as cool as a cucumber | as busy as a bee |
| as brave as a lion | as blind as a bat | as bold as brass |
| as clear as crystal | as cold as ice | as cunning as a fox |
| as deaf as a post | as dead as a dodo / doornail | as dry as a bone |
| as easy as ABC / pie | as fit as a fiddle | as flat as a pancake |
| as free as a bird | as gentle as a lamb | as good as gold |
| as hard as nails | as happy as a lark | as hungry as a wolf |
| as innocent as a lamb | as light as a feather | as meek as a lamb |
| as stubborn as a mule | as old as the hills | as playful as a kitten |
| as poor as a church mouse | as quick as lightning | as quiet as a mouse |
| as red as a beetroot | as sharp as a razor | as silent as the grave |
| as slippery as an eel | as slow as a snail | as sly as a fox |
| as smooth as silk | as sober as a judge | as steady as a rock |
| as straight as an arrow | as strong as an ox | as sweet as honey |
| as thin as a rake | as timid as a mouse | as white as snow |
| as black as coal | as wise as an owl | as fresh as a daisy |
| as graceful as a swan | as faithful as a dog | as mad as a hatter |
| as plain as day | as pretty as a picture | as regular as clockwork |
| as safe as houses | as true as steel | as warm as toast |
| as watchful as a hawk | as weak as a kitten | as vain as a peacock |
| as changeable as the weather | as greedy as a pig | as tall as a giraffe |

> **Memory trick:** group by animal. *Lamb*: gentle, innocent, meek. *Fox*: cunning, sly. *Mouse*: quiet, timid, poor (church mouse). *Peacock*: proud, vain. *Kitten*: playful, weak. The lamb and the mouse are always the soft ones.

lessons.title: Phrasal verbs (verb + particle)
lessons.body:
Changing the particle changes the meaning completely: *put off* (postpone), *put out* (extinguish), *put up with* (tolerate). Learn them in families.

| Phrasal verb | Meaning | Phrasal verb | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| back out | withdraw from a promise | bear with | be patient with |
| blow up | explode | break down | stop working; collapse emotionally |
| break into | enter by force | break out | start suddenly (war, fire, disease) |
| break up | end a relationship; disperse | bring about | cause to happen |
| bring out | publish; reveal | bring up | raise a child; mention a topic |
| brush up | revise, improve (a skill) | call for | demand, require |
| call off | cancel | call on | visit |
| carry on | continue | carry out | perform, execute |
| come across | find by chance | come by | obtain |
| come up with | produce (an idea) | count on | rely on |
| cut down on | reduce | do away with | abolish |
| drop in | visit casually | fall out | quarrel |
| fall through | fail to happen | fill in | complete (a form) |
| get along with | be friendly with | get over | recover from |
| get through | pass (an exam) | give away | distribute free; reveal |
| give in | surrender, yield | give up | stop, abandon |
| go off | explode; ring (alarm) | go through | examine; experience |
| hand over | give control to | hold on | wait |
| keep up with | stay level with | look after | take care of |
| look down on | despise | look forward to | wait eagerly for |
| look into | investigate | look up | search (dictionary); improve |
| look up to | respect, admire | make out | understand; see with difficulty |
| make up | invent; reconcile | make up for | compensate for |
| pass away | die | pass out | faint; graduate |
| point out | draw attention to | put off | postpone |
| put on | wear | put out | extinguish |
| put up with | tolerate | rule out | exclude |
| run into | meet by chance | run out of | exhaust a supply |
| see off | say goodbye at departure | see through | recognise a deception |
| set off | start a journey | set up | establish |
| show off | display boastfully | stand by | support |
| stand for | represent; tolerate | take after | resemble (a parent) |
| take in | deceive; absorb | take off | remove; (plane) rise |
| take over | assume control | take up | start (a hobby, job) |
| turn down | reject | turn out | prove to be; attend |
| turn up | arrive, appear | wear out | become useless by use; exhaust |
| wind up | close down; conclude | look out | be careful |

> **Families to learn together**
> - **put**: off (postpone), out (extinguish), on (wear), up with (tolerate)
> - **call**: off (cancel), on (visit), for (demand)
> - **look**: after (care), into (investigate), up to (respect), down on (despise), forward to (await)
> - **take**: after (resemble), off (remove), up (begin), over (control), in (deceive)
> - **break**: down (fail), into (enter by force), out (start suddenly), up (end)

examples.q:
Choose the meaning of the idiom: "To let the cat out of the bag."
(a) To free an animal (b) To reveal a secret (c) To create confusion (d) To lose something valuable
examples.solution:
Reject the literal option (a) first.
Picture it: something hidden in a bag is suddenly out, so a hidden thing becomes known.
Answer: (b) To reveal a secret

examples.q:
Complete the proverb: "Rome was not built in a ___."
(a) year (b) week (c) day (d) century
examples.solution:
Proverbs have fixed wording. The saying is "Rome was not built in a day", meaning great things take time.
"Year" or "century" may seem logical, but the fixed word is "day".
Answer: (c) day

examples.q:
Fill in the simile: "The little girl was as ___ as a lamb."
(a) proud (b) gentle (c) busy (d) sly
examples.solution:
The lamb stands for softness and innocence: gentle, meek, innocent.
Proud goes with peacock, busy with bee, sly with fox.
Answer: (b) gentle

examples.q:
Fill in the blank: "Because of the strike, the meeting has been put ___ till Monday."
(a) out (b) on (c) off (d) up
examples.solution:
"till Monday" signals postponement.
put off = postpone; put out = extinguish; put on = wear; put up = accommodate/erect.
Answer: (c) off

examples.q:
What does the underlined idiom mean? "Nobody likes him because he is always blowing his own trumpet."
(a) playing music loudly (b) boasting about himself (c) complaining (d) making excuses
examples.solution:
A trumpet announces something loudly, and it is "his own" trumpet, so he announces his own greatness.
The context "nobody likes him" supports a negative trait.
Answer: (b) boasting about himself

examples.q:
Choose the meaning of: "To get cold feet."
(a) To catch a cold (b) To become nervous and hesitate (c) To walk barefoot (d) To be very calm
examples.solution:
Literal options (a) and (c) go first.
The idiom describes someone who is about to do something (a speech, a wedding) and loses courage.
Answer: (b) To become nervous and hesitate

traps: The literal option is almost always wrong: "tie the knot" is not about rope and "under the weather" is not about rain. Eliminate it first.
Proverb and simile words are fixed by tradition, not logic: "a stitch in time saves NINE", "as fit as a FIDDLE", "as sober as a JUDGE". Do not pick a synonym that "sounds sensible".

Particles change meaning completely: call off (cancel) vs call on (visit); put off (postpone) vs put out (extinguish); look up to (respect) vs look down on (despise). Read the particle before the verb.

Look-alike idioms: "a feather in one's cap" (achievement) vs "show the white feather" (cowardice); "blue blood" (noble birth) vs "bad blood" (enmity); "at sixes and sevens" (confusion) vs "at the eleventh hour" (last moment).
Connotation matters: "hand in glove" usually implies secret or dishonest partnership, and "crocodile tears" are fake. Options with the wrong tone (positive vs negative) can be removed quickly.

practice.q: Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the idiom: A white elephant
options: A costly possession that is useless and expensive to maintain
practice.explanation: Kings of Siam are said to have gifted white elephants to courtiers they disliked: the animal was sacred, so it could not be put to work, and it cost a fortune to keep. Hook: an expensive gift you cannot use.

practice.q: Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the idiom: To bell the cat
options: To undertake a dangerous task for the common good
practice.explanation: From the fable where mice agree a bell on the cat would warn them, but no mouse dares to tie it. Hook: "Who will bell the cat?" means who will take the risk.

practice.q: Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the idiom: At sixes and sevens
practice.explanation: At sixes and sevens = in disorder, confusion ("After the transfer order, the office was at sixes and sevens"). Hook: numbers scattered about, so nothing is in order.

practice.q: Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the idiom: To burn the midnight oil
options: To light a lamp for prayers
To work or study late into the night
practice.explanation: From the days of oil lamps, when studying at midnight used up the lamp oil. Hook: the exam aspirant's idiom.

practice.q: Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the phrase: A cock-and-bull story
options: A true story from the village
practice.explanation: Cock-and-bull story = a ridiculous, invented explanation ("He told a cock-and-bull story about why he was late"). Hook: a rooster and a bull in one tale make nonsense.

practice.q: Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the idiom: To bury the hatchet
practice.explanation: Native American custom: burying the war hatchet marked the end of hostilities. Hook: put the weapon away, so the quarrel is over.

practice.q: Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the idiom: To smell a rat
options: To suspect that something is wrong
practice.explanation: Smell a rat = sense trickery or wrongdoing ("When the files went missing, the auditor smelt a rat"). Hook: a cat smells the rat before it sees it.

practice.q: Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the idiom: Hand in glove
practice.explanation: Hand in glove = very closely associated, usually in something dishonest ("The clerk was hand in glove with the smugglers"). Hook: glove and hand fit perfectly, as partners in crime do.

practice.q: Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the phrase: A dark horse
options: A little-known competitor who unexpectedly succeeds
practice.explanation: From horse racing: an unknown horse that surprises everyone by winning. Also used for a candidate. Hook: nobody saw it in the dark, until it won.

practice.q: Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the phrase: Red tape
practice.explanation: Official documents were once tied with red tape, so the phrase came to mean bureaucratic delay. Hook: files, forms and signatures.

practice.q: Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the idiom: To pay through the nose
options: To pay an excessively high price
practice.explanation: Pay through the nose = be overcharged ("Tourists paid through the nose for taxis during the festival"). Hook: it hurts, like something through the nose.

practice.q: Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the phrase: Yeoman's service
practice.explanation: Yeoman's service = very useful, loyal help ("The volunteers did yeoman's service during the floods"). Yeomen were dependable small landholders and soldiers. Hook: a yeoman is loyal and hard-working.

practice.q: Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the idiom: To throw in the towel
practice.explanation: From boxing: a boxer's corner throws a towel into the ring to concede. Same as "throw in the sponge". Hook: the towel means "we give up".

practice.q: Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the phrase: Once in a blue moon
practice.explanation: A "blue moon" is an extra full moon, which happens only about every 2–3 years. It means rarely, not never ("never" is "when pigs fly"). Hook: rare, but it does happen.

practice.q: In the sentence "Ravi was a wet blanket at the farewell party", "wet blanket" means
options: a person who spoils others' enjoyment
practice.explanation: Wet blanket = someone whose gloomy attitude spoils the fun. A wet blanket is thrown on a fire to put it out. Hook: he puts out the party's "fire".

practice.q: Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the phrase: Achilles' heel
practice.explanation: The Greek hero Achilles could be wounded only in his heel, where his mother held him when she dipped him in the river Styx. Hook: one small weak spot in a strong person.

practice.q: Complete the proverb: Too many cooks spoil the ____.
practice.explanation: Too many cooks spoil the broth = too many people handling one job ruin it. The fixed word is "broth" (soup). Hook: many cooks, one pot of broth.

practice.q: Complete the proverb: All that glitters is not ____.
practice.explanation: All that glitters is not gold = attractive appearances can be deceptive. Hook: shine is not proof of value.

practice.q: Complete the proverb: Make hay while the ____ shines.
practice.explanation: Farmers dry hay in sunshine, so make use of an opportunity while it lasts. Hook: hay needs sun.

practice.q: Complete the proverb: Don't count your chickens before they ____.
practice.explanation: Don't count your chickens before they hatch = don't rely on a result before it actually happens. Hook: not every egg becomes a chicken.

practice.q: Complete the proverb: A bird in the hand is worth two in the ____.
practice.explanation: A sure thing you already have is better than a bigger thing you might get. The fixed word is "bush". Hook: hand and bush, both short words.

practice.q: Complete the phrase: Let sleeping dogs ____.
practice.explanation: Let sleeping dogs lie = do not stir up an old problem that is quiet now. The verb is "lie" (lie-lay-lain). Hook: don't wake the dog or it may bite.

practice.q: Fill in the simile: After a month of rest, grandfather is as fit as a ____.
practice.explanation: "As fit as a fiddle" = in excellent health. The fixed partner is fiddle (a well-tuned violin). Strong goes with ox; brave goes with lion. Hook: Fit and Fiddle both start with F.

practice.q: Fill in the simile: The children sat as quiet as a ____ while the teacher read the notice.
practice.explanation: "As quiet as a mouse" is the fixed simile. Lamb goes with gentle/meek, owl with wise. Hook: the mouse is quiet, timid and poor (church mouse).

practice.q: Fill in the simile: He will never change his decision; he is as stubborn as a ____.
practice.explanation: "As stubborn (obstinate) as a mule" is the fixed pair. Ox goes with strong. Hook: a mule plants its feet and refuses to move.

practice.q: Fill in the simile: That custom is as old as the ____.
practice.explanation: "As old as the hills" = extremely old. The word is "hills", not "mountains". Hook: the H of Hills matches the H of History.

practice.q: Fill in the simile: Even at the wedding feast he remained as sober as a ____.
practice.explanation: "As sober as a judge" = completely serious, or not drunk at all. Judges are expected to be grave and clear-headed. Hook: order in court, so stay sober.

practice.q: In "The final match was called off because of heavy rain", "called off" means
practice.explanation: call off = cancel. Postpone is "put off", which is the classic confusion. Hook: call OFF means switch it OFF completely; put off means push it later.

practice.q: In "Meban takes after her mother", "takes after" means
practice.explanation: take after = resemble an older family member in looks or nature. Look after = take care of. Hook: she takes AFTER her mother because she came AFTER her and is like her.

practice.q: In "I cannot put up with his rude behaviour any longer", "put up with" means
practice.explanation: put up with = tolerate, bear. Compare put off (postpone), put out (extinguish), put on (wear). Hook: you put UP WITH a burden and carry it.
